questions.title: GATE CSE 2004 | Question: 72
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The following is the incomplete operation table of a $4-$element group.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline \textbf{*} & \textbf{e}& \textbf{a} &\textbf{b} & \textbf{c}\\\hline \textbf{e} & \text{e}& \text{a} & \text{b} & \text{c} \\\hline \textbf{a} & \text{a}& \text{b} & \text{c} & \text{e}\\\hline \textbf{b}\\\hline \textbf{c} \\\hline\end{array}$$

The last row of the table is

  1. $c\;a\;e\; b$
  2. $c\; b\; a\; e$
  3. $c\; b\; e\; a$
  4. $c\; e\; a\; b$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Powers of a yield row c,e,a,b.
review.notes: Powers of a yield row c,e,a,b.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 5
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
$n$ couples are invited to a party with the condition that every husband should be accompanied by his wife. However, a wife need not be accompanied by her husband. The number of different gatherings possible at the party is

  1. \(^{2n}\mathrm{C}_n\times 2^n\)
  2. \(3^n\)
  3. \(\frac{(2n)!}{2^n}\)
  4. \(^{2n}\mathrm{C}_n\)

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Three valid attendance states per couple yield 3^n.
review.notes: Three valid attendance states per couple yield 3^n.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 7
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the set $\Sigma^*$ of all strings over the alphabet $\Sigma = \{0, 1\}$. $\Sigma^*$ with the concatenation operator for strings

  1. does not form a group
  2. forms a non-commutative group
  3. does not have a right identity element
  4. forms a group if the empty string is removed from $\Sigma^*$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Nonempty strings have no concatenation inverse.
review.notes: Nonempty strings have no concatenation inverse.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 8, ISRO2009-53
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $\text{G}$ be an arbitrary graph with $n$ nodes and $k$ components. If a vertex is removed from $\text{G}$, the number of components in the resultant graph must necessarily lie down between

  1. $k$ and $n$
  2. $k-1$ and $k+1$
  3. $k-1$ and $n-1$
  4. $k+1$ and $n-k$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Deletion leaves k-1 through n-1 components, with isolated-vertex and star-center extremal cases.
review.notes: Deletion leaves k-1 through n-1 components, with isolated-vertex and star-center extremal cases.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 31
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $(S, \leq)$ be a partial order with two minimal elements a and b, and a maximum element c. Let P: S \(\to\) {True, False} be a predicate defined on S. Suppose that P(a) = True, P(b) = False and P(x) \(\implies\) P(y) for all $x, y \in S$ satisfying $x \leq y$, where $\implies$ stands for logical implication. Which of the following statements CANNOT be true?

  1. P(x) = True for all x \(\in\) S such that x ≠ b
  2. P(x) = False for all x \(\in\) S such that x ≠ a and x ≠ c
  3. P(x) = False for all x \(\in\) S such that b ≤ x and x ≠ c
  4. P(x) = False for all x \(\in\) S such that a ≤ x and b ≤ x

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: P(c) is forced true; the three-element witness shows only D is impossible.
review.notes: P(c) is forced true; the three-element witness shows only D is impossible.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 32
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is a valid first order formula? (Here \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are first order formulae with $x$ as their only free variable)

  1. $((∀x)[α] ⇒ (∀x)[β]) ⇒ (∀x)[α ⇒ β]$
  2. $(∀x)[α] ⇒ (∃x)[α ∧ β]$
  3. $((∀x)[α ∨ β] ⇒ (∃x)[α]) ⇒ (∀x)[α]$
  4. $(∀x)[α ⇒ β] ⇒ (((∀x)[α]) ⇒ (∀x)[β])$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Universal modus ponens proves D; countermodels falsify A-C.
review.notes: Universal modus ponens proves D; countermodels falsify A-C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 33
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following formula and its two interpretations \(I_1\) and \(I_2\).

\(\alpha: (\forall x)\left[P_x \Leftrightarrow (\forall y)\left[Q_{xy} \Leftrightarrow \neg Q_{yy} \right]\right] \Rightarrow (\forall x)\left[\neg P_x\right]\)

\(I_1\) : Domain: the set of natural numbers

\(P_x\) =  '$x$ is a prime number'

\(Q_{xy}\) = '$y$ divides $x$'

\(I_2\) : same as \(I_1\) except that \(P_x\) = '$x$ is a composite number'.

Which of the following statements is true?

  1. \(I_1\) satisfies \(\alpha\), \(I_2\) does not
  2. \(I_2\) satisfies \(\alpha\), \(I_1\) does not
  3. Neither \(I_1\) nor \(I_2\) satisfies \(\alpha\)
  4. Both \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) satisfies \(\alpha\)

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: For each x, y=1 makes the inner universal false, reducing the formula to A implies A.
review.notes: For each x, y=1 makes the inner universal false, reducing the formula to A implies A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 34
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
$m$ identical balls are to be placed in $n$ distinct bags. You are given that $m \geq kn$, where $k$ is a natural number $\geq 1$. In how many ways can the balls be placed in the bags if each bag must contain at least $k$ balls?

  1. $\left( \begin{array}{c} m - k \\ n - 1 \end{array} \right)$
  2. $\left( \begin{array}{c} m - kn + n - 1 \\ n - 1 \end{array} \right)$
  3. $\left( \begin{array}{c} m - 1 \\ n - k \end{array} \right)$
  4. $\left( \begin{array}{c} m - kn + n + k - 2 \\ n - k \end{array} \right)$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Subtract k per bag and use stars and bars.
review.notes: Subtract k per bag and use stars and bars.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 36
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
How many perfect matching are there in a complete graph of $6$ vertices?

  1. $15$
  2. $24$
  3. $30$
  4. $60$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: K6 perfect matchings count as 5*3*1.
review.notes: K6 perfect matchings count as 5*3*1.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 37
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let \(f : A \to B\) be an injective (one-to-one) function. Define \(g : 2^A \to 2^B\) as:
\(g(C) = \left \{f(x) \mid x \in C\right\} \), for all subsets $C$ of $A$.
Define \(h : 2^B \to 2^A\) as: \(h(D) = \{x \mid x \in A, f(x) \in D\}\), for all subsets $D$ of $B$. Which of the following statements is always true?

  1. \(g(h(D)) \subseteq D\)
  2. \(g(h(D)) \supseteq D\)
  3. \(g(h(D)) \cap D = \phi\)
  4. \(g(h(D)) \cap (B - D) \ne \phi\)

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: The image of the preimage is f(A) intersect D.
review.notes: The image of the preimage is f(A) intersect D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 38
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the set \(\{a, b, c\}\) with binary operators \(+\) and \(*\) defined as follows:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{+} & \textbf{a}& \textbf{b} &\textbf{c}\\\hline \textbf{a} & \text{b}& \text{a} & \text{c} \\\hline \textbf{b} & \text{a}& \text{b} & \text{c}\\\hline \textbf{c} & \text{a}& \text{c} & \text{b}\\\hline \end{array}\qquad \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{*} & \textbf{a}& \textbf{b} &\textbf{c}\\\hline \textbf{a} & \text{a}& \text{b} & \text{c} \\\hline \textbf{b} & \text{b}& \text{c} & \text{a}\\\hline \textbf{c} & \text{c}& \text{c} & \text{b}\\\hline \end{array}$$

For example, \(a + c = c, c + a = a, c * b = c\) and \(b * c = a\).

Given the following set of equations:

  • $(a * x) + (a * y) = c $
  • $(b * x) + (c * y) = c$

The number of solution(s) (i.e., pair(s) $(x, y)$ that satisfy the equations) is

  1. $0$
  2. $1$
  3. $2$
  4. $3$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Only (a,c),(b,c),(c,b) satisfy the first equation; the latter two satisfy the second.
review.notes: Only (a,c),(b,c),(c,b) satisfy the first equation; the latter two satisfy the second.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 39
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $\Sigma = \left\{a, b, c, d, e\right\}$ be an alphabet. We define an encoding scheme as follows:

$g(a) = 3, g(b) = 5, g(c) = 7, g(d) = 9, g(e) = 11$.

Let $p_i$ denote the i-th prime number $\left(p_1 = 2\right)$.

For a non-empty string $s=a_1 \dots a_n$, where each $a_i \in \Sigma$, define $f(s)= \Pi^n_{i=1}P_i^{g(a_i)}$.

For a non-empty sequence$\left \langle s_j, \dots,s_n\right \rangle$ of stings from $\Sigma^+$, define $h\left(\left \langle s_i \dots s_n\right \rangle\right)=\Pi^n_{i=1}P_i^{f\left(s_i\right)}$

Which of the following numbers is the encoding, $h$, of a non-empty sequence of strings?

  1. $2^73^75^7$

  2. $2^83^85^8$

  3. $2^93^95^9$

  4. $2^{10}3^{10}5^{10}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Only exponent 8 can be f(s); f(a)=8 and the three-string sequence gives B.
review.notes: Only exponent 8 can be f(s); f(a)=8 and the three-string sequence gives B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 40
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A graph $G=(V,E)$ satisfies $\mid E \mid \leq 3 \mid V \mid  - 6$. The min-degree of $G$ is defined as $\min_{v\in V}\left\{ \text{degree }(v)\right \}$. Therefore, min-degree of $G$ cannot be 

  1. $3$
  2. $4$
  3. $5$
  4. $6$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Degree sum at least 6|V| contradicts the edge bound.
review.notes: Degree sum at least 6|V| contradicts the edge bound.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 41
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following system of linear equations $$\left( \begin{array}{ccc} 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 4 & 3 & -12 \\ 1 & 2 & -8 \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{ccc} x \\ y \\ z \end{array} \right) = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} \alpha \\ 5 \\ 7 \end{array} \right)$$ Notice that the second and the third columns of the coefficient matrix are linearly dependent. For how many values of $\alpha$, does this system of equations have infinitely many solutions?

  1. \(0\)
  2. \(1\)
  3. \(2\)
  4. \(3\)

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Consistency forces alpha=1/5; rank 2 with three unknowns gives infinitely many solutions.
review.notes: Consistency forces alpha=1/5; rank 2 with three unknowns gives infinitely many solutions.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 60, ISRO2007-45
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A program consists of two modules executed sequentially. Let $f_1(t)$ and $f_2(t)$ respectively denote the probability density functions of time taken to execute the two modules. The probability density function of the overall time taken to execute the program is given by 

  1. $f_1(t)+f_2(t)$

  2. $\int_0^t f_1(x)f_2(x)dx$

  3. $\int_0^t f_1(x)f_2(t-x)dx$

  4. $\max\{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Independent nonnegative times sum by convolution.
review.notes: Independent nonnegative times sum by convolution.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2003 | Question: 72
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The following resolution rule is used in logic programming.
Derive clause $(P \vee Q)$ from clauses $(P\vee R),(Q \vee ¬R)$
Which of the following statements related to this rule is FALSE?

  1. $((P ∨ R)∧(Q ∨ ¬R))⇒(P ∨ Q)$ is logically valid
  2. $(P ∨ Q)⇒((P ∨ R)∧(Q ∨ ¬R))$ is logically valid
  3. $(P ∨ Q)$ is satisfiable if and only if $(P ∨ R)∧(Q ∨ ¬R)$ is satisfiable
  4. $(P ∨ Q)⇒ \text{FALSE}$ if and only if both $P$ and $Q$ are unsatisfiable

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ("verified_reference_key") cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: A is the resolution implication; B's converse fails at T,F,T; C,D are true.
review.notes: A is the resolution implication; B's converse fails at T,F,T; C,D are true.

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics

The rank of the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is

questions.title: GATE CSE 2002 | Question: 1.4
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The minimum number of colours required to colour the vertices of a cycle with $n$ nodes in such a way that no two adjacent nodes have the same colour is

  1. $2$
  2. $3$
  3. $4$
  4. $n-2 \left \lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right \rfloor+2$

questions.title: GATE CSE 2002 | Question: 1.6
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is true?

  1. The set of all rational negative numbers forms a group under multiplication.
  2. The set of all non-singular matrices forms a group under multiplication.
  3. The set of all matrices forms a group under multiplication.
  4. Both B and C are true.

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ({"pdf":"volume1","page":79,"line_index":[35]}) cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2002 | Question: 1.8
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
"If $X$ then $Y$ unless $Z$" is represented by which of the following formulas in propositional logic? ("$\neg$" is negation, "$\land$" is conjunction, and "$\rightarrow$" is implication)

  1. $(X\land \neg Z) \rightarrow Y$
  2. $(X \land Y) \rightarrow \neg Z$
  3. $X \rightarrow(Y\land \neg Z)$
  4. $(X \rightarrow Y)\land \neg Z$

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ({"pdf":"volume1","page":47,"line_index":[24]}) cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: Unless expresses (X and not Z) implies Y.
review.notes: Unless expresses (X and not Z) implies Y.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2002 | Question: 1.25, ISRO2008-30, ISRO2016-6

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 1.1

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 1.2
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following relations:

  • $R_1\:(a,b)$ iff $(a+b)$ is even over the set of integers
  • $R_2 \:(a,b)$ iff $(a+b)$ is odd over the set of integers
  • $R_3 \:(a,b)$ iff $a.b > 0$ over the set of non-zero rational numbers
  • $R_4\:(a,b)$ iff $|a-b| \leq 2$ over the set of natural numbers

Which of the following statements is correct?

  1. $R_1$ and $R_2$ are equivalence relations, $R_3$ and $R_4$ are not
  2. $R_1$ and $R_3$ are equivalence relations, $R_2$ and $R_4$ are not
  3. $R_1$ and $R_4$ are equivalence relations, $R_2$ and $R_3$ are not
  4. $R_1, R_2, R_3$ and $R_4$ all are equivalence relations

review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record ({"pdf":"manual_patch","page":0,"line_index":[]}) cross-checked against displayed question and independent derivation; no answer key changed.
review.independentCheck: R1 is equal parity, R3 equal sign; R2 and R4 fail reflexivity/transitivity.
review.notes: R1 is equal parity, R3 equal sign; R2 and R4 fail reflexivity/transitivity.
